title: Continent Finder: Which Continent Is It On?
description: Resolve any location to its continent with the Continent Finder — including the edge cases maps argue about. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a point in Istanbul resolves to a city on two continents — the Finder gives the location's continental region and the honesty the Bosphorus deserves.
quick_answer: The Continent Finder resolves a location — searched, clicked or from your position — to its continental region, using map and geocoding context. Locate the point and read the continent, with the edge cases (transcontinental countries, islands, overseas territories) treated as the genuinely interesting questions they are.

“My third continent” is a claim the Finder audits. Island nations and territories count by the rules you choose — see the FAQs.
The Bosphorus, the Urals, Suez: the questions that start arguments end here, with the reasoning shown.
Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus: Europe on the west bank, Asia on the east. The point you click decides — which is the only honest way the question can be answered.
The Sinai lies east of the Suez Canal in Asia while the rest of Egypt is African. One country, two continents, no contradiction — geography is under no obligation to be tidy.

faq: What about island states?
Islands are assigned by the continental scheme in use — usually the nearest continent or the UN geoscheme's region. Distant islands are where conventions differ most; the Finder shows its working.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — search or click any point on earth. Your own position is one optional input among three.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Continental boundaries are conventions: the Urals line, Suez, and the Caucasus are all drawn slightly differently by different authorities.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No — if you use your position, it is used for the lookup and not kept.
Seven continents or fewer?
Schools differ (some teach six, combining Europe and Asia as Eurasia). The Finder uses the seven-continent model common in US and European atlases.
Is Central America its own continent?
In the seven-continent model, no — it belongs to North America. The feeling that it is separate is cultural, and the Finder will not pretend otherwise.
Antarctica with no country?
Points there resolve to Antarctica, population: research stations. The Finder answers geography, not sovereignty.
Where does the Caucasus line run?
Authorities split Europe and Asia along the Caucasus watershed or the Kuma-Manych depression — the classic 'it depends' of continental geography, flagged here honestly.
Greenland — North America or Europe?
Geographically North America, politically Denmark. The Finder answers geography first and notes the politics.
What about points in the ocean?
Far-ocean points belong to no continent; the nearest land's answer is shown for what it is — proximity, not membership.
